stories.summary: The Electronic Frontier Foundation joined an amicus brief urging the D.C. Circuit to strike down an FAA drone flight restriction that effectively criminalized recording Department of Homeland Security and immigration agents, arguing it violates First Amendment protections for journalism and documentation of law enforcement. The brief contends that drones are essential tools for capturing unique perspectives of newsworthy events and government accountability, and that the FAA's restriction appears to be a content-based ban specifically targeting immigration enforcement documentation. The case, Levine v. FAA, is significant because even though the FAA rescinded the restriction, the court should vacate it to prevent reinstatement and establish that the government cannot use regulations to avoid accountability for punishing those exercising free speech rights.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: X-Twilio-Signature validation fails for TwiML App webhook (Voice JS SDK client call, custom params) — verified URL/token/params are all correct

Using twilio-python's official RequestValidator (v9.11.1). I've exhaustively ruled out the usual causes: The exact URL I validate against is byte-identical (SHA-256 compared) to the URL Twilio itself reports in the Console error message ("Got HTTP 403 response to https://..."). Twilio's own "Request Inspector" in the Call Log shows the exact params it sent — they match, field for field, what my server actually received (AccountSid, ApiVersion, ApplicationSid, CallSid, CallStatus, Called, Caller, Direction, From, To, plus one custom param). I brute-forced every one of the 2^11 possible subsets of those 11 received params against the received X-Twilio-Signature using RequestValidator.compute_signature(). None of the 2048 combinations reproduce it. No duplicate form keys, Content-Length matches the received body size. Account is on the IE1 (Ireland) region/edge. Has anyone seen X-Twilio-Signature validation fail specifically for TwiML App webhooks triggered by Client SDK connect() calls carrying custom parameters, despite URL, token, and params all being provably correct? Is there a known difference in how the signature is computed for this call path vs a standard REST-API-initiated call?

Why would turning on the Cloudflare proxy cause this massive 20-second delay / 522 errors while direct connection to the origin server is super fast? Any ideas or things I should check? Thanks!
